patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid drooping of decades duration initially diagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia — now worsening with new fatigability
patient.hpi:
A 53-year-old Ghanaian woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of worsening bilateral eyelid ptosis and increasing generalized fatigue. She first noticed left upper eyelid drooping at approximately age 20, which gradually worsened over years and was eventually followed by bilateral ptosis. She reported no diplopia, diurnal variation, dysphagia, or other muscle weakness throughout this time. She had multiple prior evaluations, and the consistent clinical picture — gradual onset without fatigability, no diplopia, absent ice pack test response at initial evaluation — led to a clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO).

Over the past 8 months, however, she noticed new and different symptoms: significant fatigue with prolonged talking or chewing, muffled voice quality that was worse in the afternoon, and difficulty completing her usual 30-minute walk due to bilateral leg fatigue. She also experienced occasional choking with liquids. Crucially, she noted for the first time that the eyelid drooping seemed more pronounced when tired and somewhat better in the morning — a pattern she had not observed before. She also reported a sensation of double images on lateral gaze, which resolved with eye closure.

Her ocular history included bilateral elevated intraocular pressures (managed with timolol eye drops) and bilateral cataract surgery 3 years prior (significant improvement in acuity post-operatively). She had no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease. On examination, complete bilateral ptosis was present. The ice pack test produced a 4 mm improvement bilaterally, which was POSITIVE — in contrast to prior documented negative result. Restricted extraocular movements were present, more pronounced in vertical gaze. A new finding was fatigable palate elevation on the SLURP test, absent in prior evaluations.
pmh: Elevated intraocular pressures (ocular hypertension), managed with timolol eye drops
Prior clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)

family_history: Mother had hypertension and type 2 diabetes; no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease; no family history of similar ocular disease

social_history.note: Teacher; married with three adult children; non-smoker; no alcohol; originally from Ghana, resident in UK for 18 years

physical_exam.general: Well-appearing middle-aged woman; alert and cooperative; bilateral ptosis visible immediately
physical_exam.neurological: Complete bilateral ptosis (left > right). Positive ice pack test (4 mm improvement bilaterally in 5 minutes). Extraocular movements restricted in all directions, more so in vertical gaze; no ophthalmoplegia pain. Diplopia elicitable on extreme lateral gaze but not in primary position. Fatigable palate elevation on SLURP test (new finding). No tongue fasciculations. Limb strength: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally (fatigable), otherwise 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric. Cerebellar examination normal. Sensation intact throughout. Gait normal.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.abdomen: Soft; mild central adiposity; no organomegaly
physical_exam.extremities: No edema; bilateral posterior subcapsular lens opacity noted by patient (post-cataract surgery)

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: AChR antibody–positive generalized myasthenia gravis, evolving from decades-long ocular presentation misdiagnosed as CPEO (G70.01)

differential.key_features: Prior diagnosis; however, positive ice pack test, new fatigability, diurnal variation, and positive AChR antibodies definitively exclude CPEO
differential.distinguishing_test: Ice pack test (positive), AChR antibody (positive), SFEMG (NMJ dysfunction), ECG (no heart block)

differential.key_features: No pigmentary retinopathy, no cardiac conduction defect, no cerebellar ataxia — cannot diagnose KSS; criteria not met
differential.distinguishing_test: ECG (no heart block), fundoscopy (no pigmentary retinopathy), CSF protein if needed

differential.key_features: Myotonic dystrophy can cause ptosis but also causes myotonia, grip release difficulty, cataracts, frontal balding; no these features; normal CK
differential.distinguishing_test: Myotonic discharge on EMG, DMPK gene testing if suspected

differential.key_features: Normal TSH; ptosis (not lid retraction); no proptosis; normal orbital MRI extraocular muscles
differential.distinguishing_test: Thyroid function (normal), orbital MRI (no EOM enlargement)

optimal_actions.action: Reassess ice pack test — positive result changes prior CPEO diagnosis
MG antibody panel (AChR binding, blocking, modulating, anti-MuSK)
SFEMG and RNS to confirm NMJ dysfunction
Recognize timolol eye drops as MG exacerbant and discontinue — switch to latanoprost or dorzolamide
Initiate pyridostigmine; add prednisone and azathioprine for generalized MG management

critical_actions: Recognize that positive ice pack test invalidates prior CPEO diagnosis — it is >97% specific for MG
Order AChR antibody panel as definitive serological diagnosis
Identify and discontinue timolol eye drops — beta-blockers exacerbate MG
Screen for thymoma with CT chest despite age >50 (thymus involuted but still relevant)
Assess for fatigable limb weakness — confirms generalized rather than ocular-only disease
Mitochondrial workup deferred given positive serology — AChR antibody is diagnostic
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue timolol eye drops — contraindicated in MG
Do not prescribe beta-blockers in any form without considering MG risk
Do not pursue muscle biopsy for mitochondrial disease before ordering AChR antibody (unnecessary if AChR positive)
Do not diagnose CPEO in a patient with positive ice pack test and AChR antibodies
key_reasoning_points: The diagnostic puzzle: decades-long 'CPEO' diagnosis was incorrect; the key change is a NOW-positive ice pack test and new fatigability, which should trigger AChR antibody testing
CPEO and MG can share features (bilateral ptosis, ophthalmoplegia) but are distinguished by fatigability, diurnal variation, ice pack test, and AChR antibody
Timolol eye drops are a critical hidden drug-disease interaction that may have been worsening MG for years — beta-blockers impair NMJ transmission
KSS criteria not met: no pigmentary retinopathy, no cardiac conduction defect, no cerebellar ataxia
Positive AChR antibody is the single most valuable test: >99% specific for MG if markedly elevated; precludes need for muscle biopsy
Late-onset MG can first present with pure ocular features before evolving to generalized disease years later

red_herrings.finding: Prior CPEO diagnosis over 30 years — anchoring bias
red_herrings.why_misleading: Long-standing prior diagnosis creates anchoring bias toward continuing the CPEO label despite new clinical features
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Positive ice pack test + new fatigability + AChR antibody = MG; prior CPEO diagnosis was incorrect

red_herrings.finding: Borderline lactate/pyruvate ratio suggesting possible mitochondrial disease
red_herrings.why_misleading: Borderline L/P ratio with CPEO history increases suspicion for mitochondrial myopathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Serum lactate is normal; borderline L/P ratio is non-specific; definitive AChR antibody supersedes mitochondrial concern

red_herrings.finding: Timolol eye drops as incidental medication
red_herrings.why_misleading: Topical medications often overlooked; timolol seems innocuous for ocular hypertension management
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Topical timolol has systemic absorption and is contraindicated in MG — may have been exacerbating disease for years

metadata.condition_name: Myasthenia gravis misdiagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: prior CPEO diagnosis creates anchoring bias; new fatigability and positive ice pack test are the pivotal clues; timolol eye drops as hidden contributing drug-disease interaction

mri.impression: Mild bilateral EOM volume reduction; no signal abnormality; no MRI features of MELAS or Kearns-Sayre; no orbital lesion. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings:
ELECTROCARDIOGRAM

Patient: 53-year-old female
Indication: Kearns-Sayre syndrome screen (cardiac conduction defect); new CPEO reevaluation

RHYTHM: Sinus rhythm at 64 bpm
INTERVALS: PR 162 ms, QRS 88 ms, QTc 412 ms
AXIS: Normal at +35 degrees

INTERPRETATION:
- Normal sinus rhythm
- No AV block, no bundle branch block
- No cardiac conduction defect
- QTc normal (note: timolol eye drops contribute a small systemic beta-blocker effect)

NOTE: Absence of cardiac conduction defect significantly lowers likelihood of Kearns-Sayre syndrome (KSS requires: onset <20 yrs, CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy, plus EITHER heart block, cerebellar ataxia, or CSF protein >100).

CONCLUSION: Normal ECG; no cardiac conduction abnormality.

additional_observations:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: MG re-evaluation; exclude thymoma

TECHNIQUE: CT chest with IV contrast, 1mm reconstructions

FINDINGS:
  ANTERIOR MEDIASTINUM: No thymic mass. Age-appropriate fatty involution of thymus.
  LUNGS: No parenchymal masses, no consolidation, no pleural effusion.
  MEDIASTINUM: No adenopathy.
  BONES: No lytic or sclerotic lesions.

IMPRESSION:
1. No thymoma or other mediastinal mass.
2. Age-appropriate thymic involution.

CONCLUSION: CT chest is normal. Absence of thymoma reduces but does not eliminate risk of thymoma-associated MG in older patients. Serology is diagnostic.
ct.impression: No thymoma; age-appropriate thymic involution; normal lungs and mediastinum

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — ORBICULARIS OCULI

Indication: Re-evaluate bilateral ptosis; distinguish MG from mitochondrial myopathy

RESULTS:
  MCD: 58 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
  Blocking: 18% of potential pairs
  Fiber density: 2.1 (mildly elevated, borderline)

NOTE: Mildly elevated fiber density could represent chronic denervation-reinnervation from long-standing ptosis. However, MCD is primarily increased due to NMJ transmission failure (not axonal/myopathic), consistent with MG.

MITOCHONDRIAL MYOPATHY NOTE: In mitochondrial myopathy (CPEO), SFEMG may show mildly increased jitter from myopathic changes; however, the degree of blocking and MCD abnormality here exceeds what is expected for a myopathic cause.

CONCLUSION: SFEMG confirms NMJ dysfunction as primary etiology. MG confirmed.

output.impression: SFEMG: MCD 58 µs with 18% blocking — NMJ dysfunction; degree of abnormality exceeds mitochondrial myopathy pattern

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: NMJ dysfunction evaluation in suspected MG

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS, orbicularis oculi, nasalis, deltoid

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 16% [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Nasalis: Decrement 13% ABNORMAL
  Deltoid (proximal): Decrement 11% ABNORMAL

NOTE: Abnormal decremental response in BOTH cranial and proximal limb muscles confirms generalized NMJ dysfunction, consistent with generalized MG rather than isolated ocular MG.

CONCLUSION: Generalized NMJ dysfunction confirmed by RNS in multiple muscle groups.

output.impression: RNS: 16% decrement orbicularis, 13% nasalis, 11% deltoid — generalized NMJ dysfunction consistent with generalized MG

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: CPEO vs Ocular MG — Diagnostic Pitfalls

KEY FINDINGS:
1. ICE PACK TEST: Sensitivity 80%, specificity 97% for MG ptosis when positive. Can be negative early in MG.
2. CPEO FEATURES: Symmetric, slowly progressive, no diurnal variation, negative ice pack test, elevated CK or abnormal muscle biopsy in some, maternal inheritance pattern, associated pigmentary retinopathy in KSS
3. MG FEATURES: Positive ice pack test, fatigability, diurnal variation (worse in afternoon), AChR antibodies, abnormal RNS/SFEMG
4. DIAGNOSTIC ERROR: MG can be initially diagnosed as CPEO when early features are atypical; fatigability may develop years later as disease evolves
5. TIMOLOL EYE DROPS AND MG: Beta-blockers including topical timolol can exacerbate myasthenia gravis by interfering with neuromuscular transmission. Timolol should be switched to prostaglandin analog or carbonic anhydrase inhibitor in MG patients.

IMPORTANT NOTE: This patient is on timolol eye drops for ocular hypertension — timolol may be exacerbating MG symptoms and should be discontinued/replaced.

CONCLUSION: Prior CPEO diagnosis was incorrect. AChR antibody positivity and new fatigability confirm MG. Switch timolol to alternative IOP-lowering agent.
output.summary: CPEO vs MG: ice pack test, fatigability, and AChR antibody are distinguishing features; timolol eye drops contraindicated in MG

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — TIMOLOL EYE DROPS AND MYASTHENIA GRAVIS

Query: Beta-blocker timolol (ophthalmic) in patient with confirmed MG

FINDINGS:
  TIMOLOL (topical beta-blocker):
  - Systemic absorption occurs even with topical administration (~60-70% absorbed via nasolacrimal duct)
  - Beta-blockers can impair neuromuscular transmission — mechanism: reduced presynaptic acetylcholine release through adrenergic modulation
  - Multiple case reports and case series of beta-blocker–exacerbated MG, including topical timolol
  - FDA black box warning equivalent: beta-blockers should be used with extreme caution in MG
  - Effect is dose-dependent; 0.5% timolol BID achieves significant systemic levels

RECOMMENDATION:
  Switch timolol 0.5% to preservative-free latanoprost 0.005% once daily (prostaglandin analog, no neuromuscular effects) OR
  Dorzolamide 2% BID (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, no NMJ interaction)
  Ophthalmology referral for IOP reassessment after MG treatment initiated

CONCLUSION: Timolol eye drops should be DISCONTINUED and replaced with an alternative IOP-lowering agent. This medication may have been contributing to MG symptom exacerbation.
output.summary: Timolol contraindicated in MG — switch to latanoprost or dorzolamide; systemic absorption causes beta-blocker NMJ impairment
